# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical Reading of the 24-Month Follow-up (Varden County and Halden Subset)

This is the most useful document in the series. It answers the open questions directly: whether the gain lasts, whether timesheets missed unrecorded work, and whether the meetings explanation holds up. It also corrects both the re-analysis and the meta-analysis on specific points.

The arithmetic checks out:

- 0.966/0.88 ≈ +9.8%
- 0.966/0.89 ≈ +8.5%
- Halden: 0.968/0.866 ≈ +11.8%
- 47% + 18% + 35% = 100%

However, the summary overstates the decay of the gain and the strength of the mediation result. And an event the authors report as a side observation affects the main estimate.

## 1. The control offices that cut meetings affect the decay estimate

In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their meetings, and their output per hour then rose 4.1%. That is contamination of the control group, and it matters:

- **It shrinks the measured gain.** If two of seven controls improved by about 4%, the control average rises by about 1.2 points over the later period. The difference-in-differences gain shrinks by roughly that much.
- **Some of the "fading" may be the controls improving.** Part of the fall from 12.5% to 9.8% may come from the control group getting better, not from the treated offices declining.

The paper reports this event only as a hint that reorganisation might work without cutting hours. Its effect on the main estimate isn't discussed. A sensitivity analysis that excludes those two offices, or cuts the series at month 15, would show how much of the decline is real.

There is also a puzzle in the control meeting figures. Two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, yet the control average moved only from 7.2 to 7.0. For that to work, the other five offices must have *increased* their meeting time, or the two auditing offices drifted back by month 24. The authors should say which.

## 2. The summary mixes two hours measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". The 12.5% figure is based on timesheets, and the 8.5% figure on system logs. Comparing like with like:

| Measure | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Timesheet-based gain | 12.5% | 9.8% |
| Log-based gain | not measured | 8.5% |

The body of the paper makes the correct comparison. The summary makes the decline look about 50% larger than it is.

The confidence intervals also overlap heavily: 6.9 to 18.4 at nine months, and 4.6 to 15.2 at 24 months. A decline is plausible, but the trial doesn't establish it statistically. "Declined by about a quarter" is a point estimate and should be presented as uncertain.

## 3. What do the system logs actually measure?

The logs are described as "active log-in time on the case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases". Whether this includes meetings matters for interpreting the results:

- **If logs capture only case work, two things don't fit.**
  - Treated offices cut meetings by about 3.3 hours relative to control. Their non-meeting time would then have fallen only about 3%, not the 11% the logs show.
  - Cutting meetings would not shrink the log-based denominator, so the 47% meetings share would be hard to explain. It would need a different mechanism, such as fewer interruptions breaking up the day.
- **If logs capture the whole working day, the results fit together.** But then the description is inaccurate.

The paper also calls logs the "stricter measure" and says they "show slightly more work". In fact it compares *percentage changes* (−11% against −12%), not levels. This needs clarifying before the 8.5% figure can be read as a better estimate than 9.8%.

## 4. The mediation test is pre-specified, not an independent replication

Registering the test was a real improvement over the nine-month exploratory analysis. But the summary's word "confirms" overstates what it can show:

- **The test reused the data that generated the idea.** It was registered at month 11, after the nine-month results and the meetings correlation were known. It was run on the same seven treated offices that suggested the hypothesis, and probably on months already seen.
- **"Office-months" add little independent information.** Repeated months from the same 14 offices are highly correlated. The real sample size is still about 14 clusters, and intervals like 28–66% may be too narrow if this wasn't handled.
- **Mediation shares are fragile.** The authors acknowledge confounding between mediators and the outcome. In addition, meetings and fatigue are probably linked, since fewer meetings may themselves reduce fatigue. The way the gain is split between them depends on the model, and the fatigue share (2–34%) barely excludes zero.

The body's wording, "survives a registered test", is accurate. The re-analysis's dismissal of the meetings hypothesis as "post hoc" now looks too strong. Still, the hypothesis is better supported, not confirmed. Two contaminated control offices don't show that reorganising without cutting hours would work either, and the authors say so.

## 5. The counter arm: stronger evidence, one figure unexplained

- **The concern about missing controls is now addressed.** The 7.3 against 4.0 minute waits are compared with control offices, which fixes the earlier problem that waits were reported only for treated offices.
- **The cost figure needs explaining.** Adding 12% more staff to get back to about control output (1.12 × 0.886 ≈ 0.99) raises labour cost per contact by about 13%. The stated +9% only fits if labour is about 70% of total cost. The paper should say how the figure was derived, and note that it is the county's estimate, not a trial result.

## 6. Issues raised earlier and still unanswered

- **Backlogs and time to decision.** The nine-month report flagged the risk that backlogs could build beyond statutory deadlines, but 24-month case backlogs are still not reported. That is the measure that would show whether keeping output per employee near −3.4% is putting pressure on service.
- **Overtime and total cost.** Neither is reported for case-processing, even though about 3 hours a week of overtime continued.
- **Sick days and resignations.**
  - Sick days fell 27%. The paper still doesn't say whether the 30-hour week meant fewer days, which would cause part of that fall automatically.
  - Resignations are still reported without confidence intervals.

## 7. The Halden follow-up is framed generously

- **A "marketing agency citing client deadlines" doesn't fit "coverage obligations".** Under the meta-analysis's coding, a marketing agency is discretionary work. The summary's phrase "client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches to include it. That reversion suggests some discretionary work also struggles, which slightly weakens the clean split between work types.
- **"Upper bound" is too precise a term.** The authors rightly call these 11 organisations "survivors twice over", and only 14 of 23 even agreed to respond. But there are also two years of general trends, such as new tools, wider productivity growth and staff changes, measured against a pre-pilot baseline with no control group. The estimate is probably biased upward, but nothing makes it a strict bound.
- **Possible conflict of interest.** A Halden author co-wrote this follow-up. The text is appropriately cautious, but readers should know.

## 8. The rebuttals of earlier documents mostly hold

- **Against "entirely an artifact".** The case is sound. The 24-month estimate meets the re-analysis's own standards and excludes zero. The control contamination in section 1 would, if anything, make the true gain larger, so it strengthens this rebuttal.
- **Against "no sign of decay".** Showing that all four long studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours is decisive. It matches the concern raised about the meta-analysis's duration claim. The counter-example offered, the Varden decline, is real but smaller and less certain than presented, as sections 1–2 explain.

## Where the four documents now leave the question

1. **Discretionary work.** A real gain in output per actual hour of roughly 8–10% persists at two years under a randomised design. It may be smaller than at nine months, though the decline may be partly due to control contamination.
2. **Per-worker output in discretionary work.** It is slightly below control, at about −3%, with the interval including zero. The cost per case rises modestly, and backlog and overtime costs are still unmeasured.
3. **Coverage-bound work.** Output and service fall clearly, and restoring them needs extra staff. The one randomised counter arm was stopped.
4. **Mechanism.** Cutting meetings is the leading explanation, with a smaller role for fatigue and about a third of the gain unexplained. Whether reorganising without cutting hours captures the same gain remains untested, and a fourth arm doing exactly that is the obvious next trial.
